title: Ingestion
summary: Ingestion is the first stage of the pipeline: it turns files on disk or uploaded bytes into a list of `Page` objects, each holding a document name, a page number and clean text. It reads PDFs with pypdf (one `Page` per PDF page) and TXT/Markdown as a single page, cleans the text, and joins PDF line wraps. It also enforces upload limits, because files from the API are untrusted and a huge file could exhaust memory or CPU.

key_ideas.term: Page as the unit of citation
key_ideas.explain: Keeping the page number from the very start is what lets an answer later say "travel-policy.en.pdf, page 2". Information you drop at ingest cannot be recovered later.
PDF text extraction returns the visual lines of the page, so a single sentence arrives split by hard newlines. Joining those wraps gives the sentence splitter and the embedder whole sentences.
Any endpoint that accepts files needs caps on count, size and work (PDF pages). Without them one request can fill memory or keep the server busy for minutes, a simple denial of service.
`@dataclass(frozen=True)` generates `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__`, and makes instances immutable, so a `Page` cannot be changed after it is built.

blocks.note: Module docstring: load PDF, TXT and Markdown into pages of clean text, with limits for untrusted uploads.
`from __future__ import annotations` makes every type hint a lazy string. You can then write `list[str]` or `str | None` on older Pythons (3.8, 3.9) and name a class inside its own body.

Imports `clean_text`, the readable cleanup from `rag/normalize.py`. Ingest stores readable text, not the matching form.
The set of accepted file extensions. A `set` makes the `in` check fast and the error message can list them sorted.
Comment explaining the trust model: uploads (API, Space) get all limits; local folders loaded with `load_directory` are trusted, so only the PDF page cap applies to them.
Maximum number of files per upload request, default 5. `os.getenv` returns a string (or the default string), so it is wrapped in `int(...)`. The value is read once, at import time.

Maximum bytes per uploaded file, default 10 MB (`10 * 1024 * 1024`). The default is wrapped in `str(...)` so that both the environment value and the default are strings that `int` parses the same way.
Maximum number of PDF pages, default 200. Page count is a better measure of PDF work than byte size: a small file can contain many pages of text to extract and embed. Lines 19 and 20 are blank.

`UploadTooLarge` is a custom exception that subclasses `ValueError`. A dedicated type lets the API catch exactly this case and answer HTTP 413, while other errors still surface normally. The docstring is the whole class body.

Comment explaining the wrap rule: a newline followed by a lowercase letter, digit or opening bracket, and not preceded by sentence punctuation, is a line wrap inside a sentence, not a paragraph or heading break.

The regex. `(?<![.!?:؟])` is a **negative lookbehind**: the newline must not follow a full stop, !, ?, colon or the Arabic question mark ؟. `(?=[a-z0-9(])` is a **lookahead**: the next character must be lowercase Latin, a digit or `(`. Lookarounds check context without consuming it, so only the newline itself is replaced. Arabic has no lowercase, so Arabic PDF lines are never joined by this rule (the README notes Arabic PDFs are a known limit anyway). Lines 28 and 29 are blank.
`unwrap_lines` replaces each wrap newline with a space. "employees may take 3\ndays of leave" becomes one line, so the sentence splitter later sees one sentence. Lines 32 and 33 are blank.
`@dataclass(frozen=True)` turns the class below into an immutable record with an auto-generated constructor and equality.

The PDF branch. `from pypdf import PdfReader` is a **lazy import** inside the function: the library is only loaded when a PDF is actually read, which keeps startup and tests light.

Checks the page count **before** extracting any text, so an oversized PDF is rejected cheaply and the expensive work never starts.

A list comprehension that, for every page, extracts the text, cleans it, then joins line wraps. `p.extract_text() or ""` guards against `None`/empty results, for example image-only pages. Cleaning runs before unwrapping so that spaces around newlines are already removed and the wrap regex sees a bare `\n`.

L55: builds a `Page` per page with a 1-based number. `enumerate` yields `(index, item)` pairs starting at 0, hence `i + 1`.
L56: drops pages whose text is empty (for example a scanned page with no text layer), since there is nothing to chunk or cite. Page numbers of the remaining pages stay correct because they were set before filtering.
